# Running the Loop {#sec-running-the-loop}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"In theory, there is no difference between theory and practice. But, in practice, there is."*
>
> — widely circulated aphorism
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** The aphorism fits this study, which compares a model proposal against a fixed aspect-ratio heuristic in a physical simulator. The model's explanation fails a declared distinguishing contrast. It is useful because the recorded results are less exciting than the initial hypothesis.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What must an architect fix, execute, and preserve so that one bounded AI-assisted study reaches no conclusion stronger than its recorded results?
:::

This crux addresses baseline shopping, a practical trap in AI-assisted architecture. Generative AI accelerates the creation of architectural candidates, but because simulators are configurable along many axes and models are sensitive to phrasing, it is easy to subconsciously baseline shop by tweaking simulator parameters after the fact to validate a plausible AI candidate. It is equally easy to prompt shop by silently discarding dozens of failed prompts until one produces the desired architecture. Post-hoc choices like these are the same kind that produced overoptimistic, irreproducible results across hundreds of machine-learning studies [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage].

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The Shifting Baseline"}
**The trap.** A design team celebrated a 20% architectural speedup from a novel accelerator proposal, only to discover weeks later that the baseline software was accidentally compiled without standard optimization flags (`-O3`). When the baseline was properly optimized, the entire architectural gain vanished.

**The lesson.** Unfixed baselines create illusions of progress. If the baseline is allowed to shift or remain untuned during an architectural study, any measured "improvement" is meaningless. This scenario is a composite of a recurring pattern in architecture evaluations, not a single documented incident.
:::

In a real EDA environment, the penalty for guessing wrong is large. Waiting eight hours for a physical routing failure consumes far more calendar time and limited FlexLM license checkouts than waiting ten milliseconds for a Python syntax error. This trial-and-error hides real physical costs. To combat this, the design loop must be strictly bounded.

Before any model or simulator output is known, the architect fixes the workload, legal array shapes, simulator configuration, comparison budget, rejection criteria, and decision owner. Fixing these choices prevents post-result goalpost moving and enforces discipline without claiming the choices were intrinsically optimal, serving as the baseline search strategy that an AI generative proposer must beat (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Preregister the workload, legal candidates, score, decision margin, and evaluation budget before any candidate is measured, and validate every model proposal against that legal space before it reaches the simulator.
- Report the architecture outcome, the AI contribution, the mechanism explanation, and the stopping decision as four separate judgments.
- Test a model's directional explanation against a matched contrast declared before any result is seen.
- Package a run with its provenance, inputs, and raw results so another architect can replay it, and distinguish replay from reproduction and from independent validation.

:::

## Executing the Control Case

The experiment below is a proof of concept for the automated Architecture 2.0 loop. It is deliberately modest, but it instantiates the framework on a concrete architectural problem, anchoring back to our Lighthouse prompt from @sec-moonshot to design a 3\ W, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an XR platform.

To make the problem computationally tractable for a bounded loop, we decompose that top-level system intent. We narrow the scope from the full SoC down to the XR platform's spatial tracking (SLAM) subsystem, which relies heavily on dense matrix multiplication. This partitioning is how large architectural constraints are mapped into localized AI search loops. Instead of brute-forcing all geometries, the AI proposes candidates that must clear declared gates before simulation. In a production loop those gates would include physical constraints such as die area and wiring congestion; in this run, as the protocol below records, they are schema validity, the legal dimension set, and a processing-element cap.

One recorded model call proposes three legal systolic-array datapath shapes for a compact three-layer SLAM matrix-multiplication workload. A fixed aspect-ratio heuristic proposes three shapes under the same four-call simulator budget. SCALE-Sim 3.0.0 evaluates both arms[^fn-study-arm-c08] under one frozen configuration [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3], and a declared workload contrast then tests the model's mechanism prediction. While its scope excludes model benchmarking, full-chip XR evaluation, and tapeout, it illustrates how a bounded architectural question is rigorously executed. It evaluates whether a no-change architecture result, an equal-call tie, and an unsupported mechanism explanation can be reported cleanly without being recast as an AI success. SCALE-Sim itself computes cycle counts, layer utilization, and memory traffic from an analytical dataflow model. It performs no timing closure and no physical design, and this study ran it without the energy and detailed-memory paths its version offers, so nothing here speaks to those axes; energy enters only later, as external per-access constants applied to measured traffic.

[^fn-study-arm-c08]: **Arm**: In experimental design, one of the parallel groups in a controlled comparison, as in the treatment and control arms of a clinical trial. The model and the fixed heuristic are this study's two proposal arms.

The experiment still reaches a reviewable result, although no nonbaseline shape clears the declared decision margin. The model and fixed heuristic arms tie, and the model's directional prediction fails its contrast. The recorded status-quo recommendation is to retain the 32 by 32 baseline for the five unique evaluated shapes and stop this bounded search. This shape-versus-utilization question is not a toy. Google's first TPU shipped a 256 by 256 weight-stationary[^fn-weight-stationary-c08] systolic array [@JouppiEtAl2017TPU], and its successors retreated to 128 by 128 tiles after production traffic showed the giant array too often ran partly empty, the smaller geometry proving easier to keep utilized across real workloads. One of the most widely deployed AI accelerator families changed its answer to exactly the question this study bounds, which is why the array-shape decision earns a disciplined loop rather than a default. Our 32 by 32 baseline serves as a fixed reference point rather than a claim of global optimality among all fifteen legal shapes. Another reader can inspect the proposal and rerun the recorded simulator computation without mistaking that replay for independent validation of the workload, score, or simulator.

[^fn-weight-stationary-c08]: **Weight-stationary dataflow**: A mapping in which each processing element holds one weight in place while activations stream past it and partial sums accumulate across the array. Keeping the weights still removes their memory traffic from the inner loop, which is why the array's shape rather than its raw size decides how much of it stays busy on a given layer.

Most of this procedure is familiar architecture work where an architect defines the comparison, validates tool inputs, measures candidates, tests an explanation, and decides whether the evidence warrants a change. AI participation adds a proposal and explanation whose scope, output, budget, provenance, and authority must be controlled. This integration neither changes what SCALE-Sim measured nor grants the model authority to decide what happens next.

## Preregistering the Study {#sec-executed-scale-study}

To maintain that control, preregistration fixes the terms of the study before any candidate is measured. The decision question, the judgments the record must support, and the constraints and budgets that bound the run are all declared first, so no later result can quietly redefine what would have counted as success. The declarations that follow are short, but they are what makes the study's numbers reviewable rather than curated.

### Defining the Decision

The architecture question is deliberately narrow to test a precise hypothesis without overextending the methodology.

> Under the declared local rule, does any candidate selected by the recorded
> model or fixed aspect-ratio heuristic warrant follow-up over the 32 by 32
> baseline, and does the model's directional prediction survive its declared
> contrast?

A 32 by 32 matrix unit was selected as the baseline because it is a compact, square array that maps onto the workload's GEMM[^fn-gemm-c08] layers without the utilization penalty that elongated shapes carry, and on the architect's prior that elongated shapes also cost wire length, an axis this simulator does not measure. It was not selected on any claim of optimality. The same qualification applies to the heuristic arm, and it matters more than the baseline's, because the AI-contribution judgment is a comparison against it. A fixed aspect-ratio rule is a reasonable proposer for this workload and not a strong one, so a tie against it establishes that the model did not beat a simple rule under an equal budget, and establishes nothing about how either would fare against a competent human architect. Read the tie as a bound on the claim rather than as a measure of the model. The workload contains three GEMM layers extracted from the XR platform's spatial tracking (SLAM) pipeline, serving as a compact test slice rather than a claim about a full XR application. Their (M, N, K) dimensions are 128 by 128 by 256, 64 by 192 by 128, and 32 by 128 by 192, and the mechanism test exchanges M and N in the two nonsquare layers. Printing these dimensions is what lets a later reader recompute the tie, the utilization figures, and the aspect-ratio ranking on paper. Preregistering this workload characterization prevents post-hoc substitution and makes every later claim explicitly conditional on this slice, though it cannot make the slice representative. Only the datapath's array dimensions vary, while dataflow, on-chip scratchpad capacity, interface bandwidth, layout, simulator version, workload, deadline, and scoring rule remain fixed. This narrowness isolates the effect of proposal source and array shape by holding most of the environment still. It also leaves out something a preregistration should carry. Nothing in the protocol asks whether the design could separate the arms at all, and in a fifteen-shape space under a four-call budget two competent proposers are likely to converge on the same candidates, which is what happened. A preregistration that freezes budgets and margins without asking what result would distinguish its arms can run to completion and answer a question it never had the power to ask.

[^fn-gemm-c08]: **GEMM (general matrix multiply)**: The dense matrix-matrix multiplication kernel, conventionally described by the three dimensions M, N, and K, that accounts for most of the arithmetic in a neural-network layer. An accelerator array is ultimately judged by how well its height and width fit the M, N, and K of the layers it has to run, which is why those numbers, not the layer names, are what a shape study must record.

### The Four Judgments

A candidate ranking does not answer every question in an AI-assisted architecture study, so this experiment produces four distinct judgments from different parts of the record.

- **Architecture outcome:** asks whether any evaluated nonbaseline shape clears the local decision margin over 32 by 32.
- The **AI contribution** asks whether the recorded model arm finds a better score than the fixed aspect-ratio heuristic under the same simulator-call budget.
- The **mechanism explanation** asks whether the model's directional prediction survives its declared distinguishing contrast.[^fn-planned-contrast-c08]
- The **stopping decision** asks whether another evaluation is warranted under the predeclared rule and current project scope.

[^fn-planned-contrast-c08]: **Contrast**: In the design of experiments, a specific comparison between conditions planned before the data are seen. The M/N-transposed workload is this study's planned comparison for testing the model's directional explanation.

These judgments can disagree, meaning a model might propose a competitive candidate without beating the heuristic, or a tied candidate could leave the status quo in place. A useful candidate might arrive with a failed explanation, and a bounded study can stop even though most of the legal design space remains unevaluated. The executed comparison below reports all four outcomes without combining them into a single claim that the model or the complete discipline succeeded.

### Separating Outcomes from Claims

The preregistration keeps the architecture-outcome and AI-contribution claims
separate. This deliberate decoupling enforces one rule. The AI proposes candidates, and the deterministic simulator evaluates them. The model must never be allowed to grade its own homework. This ensures that a "successful" model invocation (one that generates valid JSON or a plausible explanation) is not conflated with a successful architectural design. The study runs in stages, from preregistering the decision, through bounded candidate generation and deterministic simulation, to the decision outcomes that close it (@fig-bounded-study-workflow).

![**Judgment is decoupled from generation:** preregistration fixes the terms, bounded generation and deterministic evaluation produce the record, and only then does the study close on one of four decision outcomes. The four analytic judgments are read off that record; they are not workflow stages.](images/ch8_design_loop_workflow){#fig-bounded-study-workflow width="100%" fig-alt="Workflow diagram of a bounded study. Three stage boxes run left to right, preregistration, bounded candidate generation, and deterministic simulation, then fan out to four decision-outcome boxes: accept target, reject target, modify bounds, and abandon study."}

- **Architecture-outcome claim.** At least one evaluated nonbaseline shape
selected by either arm improves the local decision score over the 32 by 32
baseline by at least 1 percent for the frozen workload and simulator
configuration. The outcome is no change if none of those evaluated shapes
clears that decision margin.

- **AI-contribution claim.** With four SCALE-Sim evaluations per arm, including
the same mandatory baseline, the recorded model arm finds a score at least 1
percent lower than the fixed aspect-ratio heuristic arm. A difference within 1
percent is a tie. A worse model result is adverse. Equal simulator calls do not
equalize model inference, human setup, prior knowledge encoded in the heuristic,
or total labor. One model call cannot establish a population-level result about
a model family, even if it wins.

These two outcome claims were fixed before proposal generation. The mechanism
hypothesis follows a different sequence. The architect fixed a mirrored-shape
test on the original and M/N-transposed workloads, then required the model to
supply its directional prediction before any simulation.

The local score is

$$
S = \frac{\text{total cycles}}
         {\text{average layer utilization}/100},
$$

with lower values preferred. This composite is not a true Area-Delay Product (ADP). Substituting utilization $\approx \text{work}/(\text{PE}\cdot\text{cycles})$ gives $S \propto \text{PE}\cdot\text{cycles}^2/\text{work}$, so the cycle (delay) term enters squared relative to ADP; the score double-counts delay rather than penalizing underutilization as such. It serves as a predeclared selection rule for this study, not a universal measure of accelerator quality or a physical measurement. The formula does discourage degenerate solutions such as oversized arrays that remain mostly idle, though it is the 1,024-processing-element legality cap, not the score, that actually forecloses oversized arrays. Reporting cycles and utilization separately keeps the composite score from hiding the two ingredients it combines, though it cannot reveal an axis the score leaves out, such as memory traffic.

A fair comparison requires the evaluation budget, workload, simulator settings,
rejection criteria, and decision boundary to be frozen before either arm
produces results. @tbl-executed-study-protocol records those rules.

| **Element** | **Frozen rule** |
| --- | --- |
| **Workloads** | One three-layer GEMM slice, plus a versioned copy with M and N exchanged for the mechanism test. |
| **Legal shapes** | Rows and columns each in {8, 16, 32, 64, 128}; product no greater than 1,024 processing elements. These rules admit fifteen shapes. The cap is a declared scope bound for this study, chosen to keep candidates in a range plausible for a 3\ W mobile subsystem, not a limit derived from the power budget by this simulator, which was run here with no power or area model enabled. |
| **Environment** | SCALE-Sim 3.0.0, GEMM interface, weight-stationary dataflow [@ChenEtAl2016Eyeriss], 128 KiB per SRAM, and 64 interface words per cycle. |
| **Baseline and rejection criteria** | Insert 32 by 32 into both arms; reject shapes above 1,024 processing elements or runs above 90,000 cycles. |
| **Proposal arms** | Three model proposals and three candidates from a fixed aggregate-aspect-ratio heuristic. |
| **Evaluation budget** | Four SCALE-Sim evaluations per arm after inserting the baseline; no post-result replacement. |
| **Prompt development** | Log exploratory prompt iterations and total hours spent *before* preregistration to track the true human-in-the-loop cost. |
| **Model repair** | At most one complete repair response after reported schema or legality errors; invalid proposals consume the initial call. |
| **Decision margin** | At least 1 percent on the lower-is-better local score; differences inside the margin are ties. |
| **Mechanism probe** | Four shared runs comparing 16 by 64 and 64 by 16 on the original and M/N-transposed workloads. |
| **Decision boundary** | The recorded result may motivate a clearly scoped follow-up experiment or stopping. It cannot authorize RTL, tapeout, or a system intent decision. |

: **The comparison was fixed before evaluation.** Both proposal arms use the same workload, SCALE-Sim configuration, rejection criteria, baseline, and four-evaluation budget. {#tbl-executed-study-protocol tbl-colwidths="[22,68]"}

The workload, legal shapes, environment, and rejection criteria fix the
architecture comparison. The proposal and evaluation budgets prevent either
arm from receiving extra candidates after results appear. A production physical-design flow could not be bounded this way. Its stage runtimes vary by orders of magnitude, so a raw count of calls meters them badly, and such a flow budgets compute effort in CPU-hours and short-circuits weak candidates at a cheap stage such as floorplan estimation before paying for detailed routing. This study meters a single analytical stage, so the budget row records a flat four calls per arm. The repair and decision rules fix how invalid model output and small score differences will be treated. The mechanism contrast challenges the generated explanation, while
the final row leaves approval outside both the model and simulator.

Predeclaring these choices forces any change to the candidate, metric, or stopping rule out into the open, where it can be checked against the record instead of silently validating a flawed candidate.

Preregistration does not outlaw tinkering; it timestamps it. The architect is free to iterate on prompts, scores, and baselines for a week, and that exploratory phase is where most real understanding forms. The Prompt development row exists to log exactly that phase rather than to forbid it. The discipline asks only that the exploration be labeled as exploration, and that the confirmatory run which feeds a decision start after the freeze, on terms the exploration did not get to grade. Exploration generates the hypothesis; confirmation is not allowed to reuse the runs that suggested it.

Nor does preregistration intrinsically justify the
three-layer workload, local score, 32 by 32 baseline, 1 percent decision margin,
90,000-cycle cutoff, SCALE-Sim abstraction, or four-call budget. Each remains
an architecture choice that would need a rationale and sensitivity analysis
before a broader decision relied on it.

The 1 percent margin deserves one more question, 1 percent of what? SCALE-Sim's
cycle counts are not accurate to within 1 percent of silicon; no analytical model
is, and its absolute error against fabricated hardware runs orders of magnitude
larger than the margin the decision rule reads off it. The margin survives that
gap only because both arms run through the same frozen model, so the systematic
error is shared and mostly cancels when candidates are ordered against each other.
That is the standing bargain of architecture simulation. A frozen simulator
supports relative judgments between candidates it treats identically, never
absolute claims about any one of them, and the decision margin must sit above
whatever residual error does not cancel across the compared pair.

Every rule frozen in @tbl-executed-study-protocol exists because a comparison left unfixed can be adjusted after the result arrives, and nothing in the published record will show that it was. An entire research literature demonstrates the consequence at scale.

::: {.callout-war-story title="Civil-war prediction and the margin that was a leak"}
**The claim.** A series of political-science papers reported that complex machine-learning models, random forests and AdaBoost among them, substantially outperformed the decades-old logistic regression baseline at predicting the onset of civil war.

**The gap.** None of those results reproduced [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage]. Each depended on a leak between the data used to fit a model and the data used to score it, most often imputing missing values across the training and test sets together before splitting them. The published record could not separate a real margin from a procedural one, and peer review saw only the margin. Preregistration alone would not have caught this particular fault, since a leak sits inside the declared pipeline and would have been frozen along with it, which is why the survey's own remedy is documenting and auditing the pipeline. What preregistration does block is the retuning, reselection, and goalpost moving that a fixed comparison forecloses. Once the leaks were corrected, the complex models did not beat logistic regression in any of the cases. The same survey found leakage across 17 fields, affecting hundreds of papers.

**The lesson.** Fix the comparison before the result exists. A margin measured against a baseline that could still be retuned, contaminated, or reselected afterward is not a measured margin, and no amount of care in the modeling recovers it later. This study's protocol is worth its cost only because it was filled in before a single candidate ran.
:::

### The Mechanism Hypothesis

As established in @sec-data-representations-world-models, general knowledge is meaningless without explicit project constraints. The representation for this study is small, describing one accelerator under one set of fixed conditions rather than the accelerator in general. The fifteen legal shapes, baseline, mutable array dimensions, fixed simulator conditions, local score, and workload matrices form the explicit design state. Formalizing these variables keeps authority over the design boundaries with the architect. In this instance, the candidate representation changes only the datapath's `ArrayHeight` and `ArrayWidth`, while the weight-stationary dataflow [@ChenEtAl2016Eyeriss], SRAM capacity, interface bandwidth, layout, workload, and simulator version remain fixed.

That representation is useful only if a candidate change can be connected to a predicted consequence. The model proposed three shape deltas and predicted that a wider 16 by 64 array would better match the workload's N dimensions than its mirrored 64 by 16 alternative, further asserting that exchanging M and N in the workload would reverse the winner. The AI's ability to predict a directional outcome relies on its learned statistical priors, which can yield a fluent rationale that misstates the true cause of the answer [@TurpinEtAl2023Unfaithful] and therefore has to be tested against the simulator's observation rather than accepted on the strength of its explanation. The proposal therefore emitted both a design-state change and a testable consequence hypothesis that the simulator could challenge.

![**The axis binding this study never wrote down:** under SCALE-Sim's weight-stationary GEMM mode the resident weight tile is K by N, so array height carries the reduction dimension K, array width carries N, and M streams through the array rather than occupying a dimension of it. Transposing M and N therefore looks like a swap of orientation but is not one, because K stays where it is and a mirrored pair such as 16 by 64 and 64 by 16 moves the height and width fold counts together. The prompt fixed the dataflow without ever stating this binding, which is why the mechanism contrast cannot causally isolate orientation.](images/F8-array-mapping){#fig-array-mapping fig-alt="A GEMM workload box feeds a resident weight tile of K by N, which maps onto two array orientations, a wide 16 by 64 array and a tall 64 by 16 array, each labeled with K over height and N over width. A dashed transpose connector below them notes that K is unchanged, so the mirrored pair moves both fold counts."}

The record omits one important part of that connection. It names GEMM M, N, and
K dimensions and fixes SCALE-Sim's weight-stationary mode, but it does not state
how those dimensions map onto `ArrayHeight` and `ArrayWidth` under the selected
mapping. The weight tile that stays resident is K by N, which binds K to array
height and N to array width and leaves M to stream through
(@fig-array-mapping). The
model's assumption that width tracks N was therefore the conventional one, but
the prompt never pinned it, so the study cannot show that the model reasoned to
that binding rather than defaulted to it.

The deeper problem lies in the contrast itself. The transposition still distinguishes the model's exact directional prediction, but it is not a causally isolated test of orientation, because exchanging M and N leaves K untouched. A mirrored pair such as 16 by 64 and 64 by 16 therefore changes the N-fold count on the width axis and the K-fold count on the height axis at once, while M never migrates to an array dimension at all. Because the mapping was not defined in the AI prompt before inference, and because the contrast moves two fold counts together, the test probes the prompt's completeness and the contrast's design at least as much as the AI's architectural reasoning. It is not silent on that reasoning, though. The recorded global mechanism turns on how well the geometry matches each layer's M-versus-N footprint, a framing that binds rows to M and leaves K without an array dimension at all, while the model's own anticipated failure mode named K-tiling as the effect that could overturn it. A stronger follow-up must pin the mapping semantics explicitly in the prompt and choose contrasts that vary one fold count at a time.

### Fixing Environment and Roles

The completed loop card indexes every artifact of the run (@tbl-practitioner-path).

| **Card field** | **Completed study record** |
| --- | --- |
| **Decision** | Determine whether any selected nonbaseline shape warrants follow-up over 32 by 32 under the local rule, and stop with the status quo if none clears the decision margin. |
| **State and scope** | The preregistration fixes the workload, baseline, fifteen legal shapes, mutable fields, non-goals, and decision boundary. The completed comparison evaluates five unique shapes selected under those rules. |
| **Representation** | The model prompt, output schema, original workload, and transposed workload encode the available design state and consequence hypothesis. Mapping semantics between GEMM axes and array dimensions remain unspecified. |
| **Roles and actions** | The model proposes and explains. The fixed aspect-ratio heuristic proposes. Validation scripts check structure and legality. SCALE-Sim evaluates. The architect judges the four claims and retains approval authority. |
| **Budget and checks** | Each proposal arm receives four simulator calls including the baseline. Four additional calls run the declared contrast. Schema, legality, 90,000-cycle, and decision-margin checks are fixed, with no post-result replacement. |
| **Evidence** | The complete model response, all evaluations, and study result preserve proposals, measurements, claim dispositions, and the stopping status. |
| **Decision status** | The bounded search stops with 32 by 32 as the status quo for the five evaluated shapes. The architecture action remains `awaiting_author_confirmation`, and no optimality claim follows. |

: **The card indexes the record, it does not replace it:** each field points to the retained files that define the state, roles, checks, evidence, and decision status. {#tbl-practitioner-path tbl-colwidths="[21,69]"}

The role separation in @tbl-practitioner-path matters because while the model and fixed heuristic select candidates, neither produces the measured score or approves an architecture change. The validator may reject malformed or illegal output but cannot decide whether the workload or objective is appropriate. SCALE-Sim calculates the recorded quantities without establishing its own fidelity, leaving the architect to own those judgments and the final stopping decision.

## Model Calls and Failures

With the roles and constraints fixed, the architect invokes the model. It received the architecture question, legal dimension set, processing-element budget, workload matrix dimensions, fixed environment assumptions, mandatory baseline, output schema, scoring definition, and evidence boundary, but it did not receive the fixed heuristic's candidates or simulator results. The model then proposed a design mutation by naming three candidates, predicting qualitative behavior, stating an anticipated failure mode, and offering a directional mechanism with a testable failure condition. The architect evaluates this output as a candidate, not a final decision.

### Handling Toolchain Errors

The first attempt to invoke the runtime never reached inference. The response-format service rejected the request's JSON Schema before any tokens were generated.[^fn-json-schema-c08] Following the tool interface principles from @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, this schema error is classified as an infrastructure failure, which can be repaired cheaply, rather than a valid architectural constraint violation like an unroutable netlist. Toolchain failures must be isolated from architectural evaluations.

[^fn-json-schema-c08]: **JSON Schema rejection (detail)**: Two constant-string properties in the schema lacked explicit types, so no model output or usage was produced. The schema-only correction and both hashes were added as a preregistration amendment before inference.

Fixing a broken schema or a transient environment timeout is a necessary infrastructure repair, not a concession to the model or a change in the evaluation protocol. A harness driving a real toolchain would have to sort its failures more carefully than this one did, because undocumented EDA tool segfaults, FlexLM license server timeouts, and simulation deadlocks are not all infrastructure noise. Sort them on reproducibility rather than on failure type, because a tool segfault is usually deterministic and input-dependent, and no harness can tell a transient fault from a candidate-correlated one at the moment it has to act. Retry once on an unchanged input and record the outcome. A failure that clears is infrastructure; one that reproduces is candidate-correlated however it arrived, and it belongs back in the proposer's context as negative evidence about a physical boundary, as a design-rule violation or a congestion-driven place-and-route timeout plainly does. Discarding those runs as noise teaches the proposer nothing, and reading them backwards is worse still. A proposer told that a license outage was routing congestion will keep shrinking a block that was never too dense, and the search converges on a degenerate candidate that no tool ever actually rejected. The only failure this run recorded was the pre-inference schema rejection, which carried no architectural information at all, so the classification never had to be made.

The same discipline applies one level up, to what the record omits rather than what it misclassifies. A run that discards its failed attempts before writing anything down produces a study whose cost cannot be reconstructed.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The illusion of zero-shot success"}
**The trap.** An AI model generates a highly optimized architecture design on the first try, and the write-up presents the result as zero-shot capability, a first-try success with no examples or iteration.

**The mechanism.** The write-up omits the dozens of prior manual iterations in which an architect tweaked the prompt, added constraints, and fixed syntax errors. This prompt shopping hides the true human-in-the-loop cost, framing a heavily curated result as autonomous intelligence. The case here is a composite of a pattern reviewers report across AI-for-design evaluations, not one specific publication.

**The lesson.** Bounded studies must record all inference attempts, repairs, and environment failures. The true cost of a candidate includes the discarded prompts and failed runs that led to it.
:::

### Capturing Call Provenance

The subsequent call returned a schema-valid response. Since semantic validation found three unique legal candidates, no repair call was made. The complete response is retained, not only the candidate coordinates or a prose summary. The runtime exposed only part of the provenance needed to identify the call, so @tbl-model-provenance records the supplied values and marks the rest as unavailable instead of inferring them. A production EDA run would fill the execution-environment field far more heavily, pinning the PDK version, standard-cell library PVT corners,[^fn-pvt-corners-c08] binary patches, and Tcl setup scripts through Nix or containers to prevent environmental drift; this study carried none of that toolchain, so the field is recorded as empty rather than left to inference.

| **Provenance field** | **Recorded value** |
| --- | --- |
| **Provider and interface** | OpenAI through Codex CLI 0.144.4, noninteractive ephemeral execution, read-only empty workspace. |
| **Execution environment** | None beyond the runtime above; the study ran in a read-only empty workspace with no EDA toolchain, PDK, or standard-cell libraries in play. |
| **Requested and accepted model alias** | gpt-5.4; provider revision or digest was not exposed. |
| **Time** | 2026-07-14 18:21:51--18:22:24 UTC; 32.90 seconds wall time. |
| **Settings** | Medium reasoning effort; temperature, top-p, and seed were not exposed or available through the runtime. |
| **Usage** | 13,223 input tokens, including 1,920 cached; 1,446 output tokens, including 516 reasoning tokens. |
| **Cost** | Currency cost was not reported, so none is inferred. |
| **Interaction** | One valid proposal call, no repair call, and no observed tool calls. Prompt, schema, output, and provenance hashes are recorded. |
| **Privacy** | No credential, session identifier, or private configuration is stored. |

: **Provenance is only as good as the runtime exposes:** the record reports the values the runtime supplied and marks the rest as unavailable rather than inferring them. {#tbl-model-provenance tbl-colwidths="[27,63]"}

[^fn-pvt-corners-c08]: **PVT corners**: The process, voltage, and temperature extremes that a standard-cell library is characterized at, such as a slow-process, low-voltage, high-temperature combination. Cell delay and leakage change substantially from one corner to the next, so a timing or power number carries no meaning unless the corner it was measured at travels with it.

Two limits matter when interpreting this record. First, the valid proposal used one call and no repair, meaning later candidate replacement cannot explain the outcome. Evaluating generative models requires sampling multiple trajectories to measure expected utility. Future scaled iterations must adopt standard ML evaluation precedents, such as the pass@k metric [@Chen2021Codex], using non-zero temperature to measure the model's true search capability across a broader design space. Sampling more trajectories sharpens that estimate only if the checks behind it are strong, since weak test suites let incorrect candidates pass and inflate such scores [@LiuEtAl2023EvalPlus]. A space of fifteen legal shapes also caps what any such estimate could show. Separating a proposer from a simple heuristic takes a search space in which the heuristic has no obvious ordering, one that varies dataflow selection or SRAM partitioning as well as array dimensions, and the overlap between the two arms, reported in the next section, shows what the narrow space cost this comparison. Second, the requested alias is not a pinned model identity, since a hosted model behind a fixed alias can measurably shift behavior between dated snapshots [@ChenEtAl2024ChatGPTBehavior]. The response hash pins the retained output rather than the hosted generator. The record therefore verifies what happened in this call but cannot recreate the generation exactly, although the SCALE-Sim runs remain replayable from their retained inputs.

The record also stops short of one cost it declared it would track. It preserves the single clean proposal call and the one schema rejection that preceded it, but it does not log the exploratory prompt iterations and author hours spent before the protocol was frozen. A complete accounting of this study would include that human cost, and its absence here is a stated limitation rather than an oversight.

### Interpreting Proposal Overlap

The model proposed 16 by 64, 8 by 128, and 32 by 16. The fixed aspect-ratio
heuristic ranked legal shapes by processing-element count, then by closeness to
the workload's aggregate N-to-M aspect ratio, with a deterministic tie break.
It proposed 16 by 64, 8 by 128, and 64 by 16. The two arms therefore selected
two of the same nonbaseline shapes. Including the shared 32 by 32 baseline, the
union contains five unique evaluated shapes from the fifteen legal shapes.

This overlap matters because the shared choices cannot be attributed uniquely to the
model. The arms agree on two of their three proposals and differ in only one,
where the model's 32 by 16 and the heuristic's 64 by 16 each rank worse. With
only fifteen legal shapes and two competent proposers converging this closely,
the comparison had little resolving power[^fn-resolving-power-c08] to separate them from the start. A tie was the
likely outcome before either arm ran, so the result reports that limit rather
than measured parity, whatever the model's quality.

[^fn-resolving-power-c08]: **Resolving power**: A design's ability to separate genuinely different candidates. The evaluation here is deterministic and noise-free, so the limit is discrimination rather than statistical power over evaluation noise, though repeated calls to a stochastic proposer would still define a distribution of their own. With few distinct legal shapes and two proposers converging on the same candidates, no fixed contrast could have separated them, and a tie was expected regardless of the proposers' true quality.

## Reporting Selected Candidates

Every proposed candidate passed the processing-element and cycle-limit checks,
so this run does not exercise the invalid-candidate repair path, the
illegal-shape rejection, or the 90,000-cycle cutoff. Those three declared
control checks are asserted as protections but never fire on this single worked
example, which therefore demonstrates them only in the passing direction.
Showing them reject an illegal or over-cycle candidate would require a trace
this bounded run does not contain.

A check that has never fired is a claim, not a protection. The standing remedy
is a positive control, the same one every wet lab runs on every assay. Preregister
one canary alongside the real candidates, a shape that violates the
processing-element budget or a run known to blow the cycle cutoff, and require the
harness to reject it before the arms are scored. If the canary passes, the run is
invalid regardless of what the candidates did, because the study has just measured
its own control checks and found them absent.

Back in the run that did execute, several legal
alternatives ranked worse under the declared score, and no nonbaseline shape
cleared the decision margin across all eight arm evaluations
(@tbl-ai-study-results).

| **Arm** | **Shape and source** | **Cycles** | **Average layer utilization** | **Local score** | **Result within arm** |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Model | 32 by 32 baseline | 13,917 | 41.196% | 33,782.40 | Tied best |
| Model | 16 by 64 proposal | 13,917 | 41.196% | 33,782.40 | Tied best |
| Model | 8 by 128 proposal | 19,405 | 29.704% | 65,327.45 | Ranked worse |
| Model | 32 by 16 proposal | 25,277 | 45.438% | 55,629.61 | Ranked worse |
| Heuristic | 32 by 32 baseline | 13,917 | 41.196% | 33,782.40 | Tied best |
| Heuristic | 16 by 64 proposal | 13,917 | 41.196% | 33,782.40 | Tied best |
| Heuristic | 8 by 128 proposal | 19,405 | 29.704% | 65,327.45 | Ranked worse |
| Heuristic | 64 by 16 proposal | 17,757 | 32.294% | 54,985.25 | Ranked worse |

: **The model and fixed heuristic arms tie under equal simulator-call budgets.** Neither finds a nonbaseline candidate that clears the predeclared 1 percent decision margin over 32 by 32. Values are computed by SCALE-Sim, not measured on silicon. {#tbl-ai-study-results tbl-colwidths="[12,23,11,18,14,22]"}

The 16 by 64 candidate exactly matches the baseline's cycles, average layer utilization, and local score. The exact tie is not a coincidence, and the reason is narrower than equal resources, since the 8 by 128 shape has the same 1,024 processing elements yet takes 39% more cycles. For this workload the recorded per-layer cycle counts of the two tied shapes are identical for two reasons acting together. The layers fold onto 32 by 32 and 16 by 64 in the same number of tiles with no edge waste in either case, and the per-fold pipeline cost under this weight-stationary schedule, which runs as twice the array height plus the array width, comes to 96 for both. Equal tile counts alone would not produce the tie, since the heuristic's 64 by 16 shape folds into the same eighty tiles at full mapping efficiency and still takes 27.6 percent more cycles. The shapes differ only in how those tiles move data. That arithmetic fits on an index card, and it exposes an uncomfortable feature of this study. Cycles under a frozen dataflow follow the ceil-divided tile counts and edge waste of each shape, a closed-form quantity, so all fifteen legal shapes were rankable on paper before the first simulator call. A budget spent watching the simulator confirm ceil-division is a budget an analytical zeroth arm, a paper pass run before any simulator call, should have consumed for free; a call that only reproduces paper arithmetic is a spent unit. That closed-form rankability does not license a claim about the ten shapes nobody ran, and the two statements only look contradictory if prediction and evidence are treated as the same currency. The paper ranking is a prediction from a model of the dataflow. The study preregistered that its claims rest on measured runs, so a shape that was never measured stays outside the claim no matter how confidently the arithmetic ranks it. Reporting the ranking as a prediction and the five measured shapes as evidence is the honest split, and the gap between them is the argument for running the zeroth arm first rather than for widening the conclusion. Calling the candidate the new winner would improperly convert a tie into an improvement by changing the rule after seeing the output. The tie also hides a difference the score never registers.[^fn-dram-traffic] Because the local score combines only cycles and utilization, it reads the two shapes as equal while their off-chip write traffic differs by a factor of two. For a 3\ W mobile XR chip, data movement energy typically dominates compute [@Horowitz2014Energy]. This means the 16 by 64 candidate is realistically worse, being Pareto-dominated on a memory axis the simulator measured but the score ignored (@fig-proxy-mismatch). The blindness runs both ways. On that same axis the heuristic's 64 by 16 shape halves the baseline's off-chip writes and issues 31 percent fewer DRAM accesses overall, paying 27.6 percent more cycles for it, so the score ranks worse a shape an energy-first rule would rank better.

```{python}
#| label: energy-gap-computation
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

# Price the tie from the recorded study results and the Horowitz per-access
# anchors receipted in data/source-receipts/chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv
# (DRAM: 1300-2600 pJ per 64-bit access at the 45 nm anchor). The values
# regenerate from the record on every build.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
_runs = {}


def _collect(obj):
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        if obj.get("candidate_id") and "metrics" in obj:
            _runs[obj["candidate_id"]] = obj["metrics"]
        for v in obj.values():
            _collect(v)
    elif isinstance(obj, list):
        for v in obj:
            _collect(v)


with open(_root / "labs" / "examples" / "ai_systolic_array_study" / "recorded" / "reference" / "study_results.json", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _collect(json.load(fh))
_base = _runs["conventional_baseline_32x32"]["dram_accesses"]
_cand = _runs["heuristic_16x64"]["dram_accesses"]
_extra = _cand - _base
_lo_uj = _extra * 1300e-12 * 1e6
_hi_uj = _extra * 2600e-12 * 1e6
_lo_mw = _extra * 1300e-12 * 90 * 1e3
_hi_mw = _extra * 2600e-12 * 90 * 1e3
print(
    f"The record also prices the gap. The 16 by 64 candidate performs {_cand:,} "
    f"DRAM accesses to the baseline's {_base:,}, a {_cand / _base:.2f}x difference. "
    f"At Horowitz's 45 nm anchors of 1300 to 2600 pJ per 64-bit access, those "
    f"{_extra:,} extra accesses cost roughly {_lo_uj:.0f} to {_hi_uj:.0f} microjoules "
    f"more per workload pass. An energy becomes a power claim only once the pass has "
    f"a period. If the SLAM slice runs once per frame at 90 Hz, that is about "
    f"{_lo_mw:.0f} to {_hi_mw:.0f} milliwatts, under two percent of the 3\\ W envelope. "
    f"The anchors are order-of-magnitude technology constants rather than signoff "
    f"numbers, and SCALE-Sim counts interface words rather than 64-bit DRAM "
    f"transactions, so the figure overstates on both counts. The ratio is what "
    f"survives. The two designs the score called identical are not identical "
    f"in energy."
)
```

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The tie, priced against the 3 W XR subsystem"}
The doubled write traffic is not only a power number. The SLAM subsystem shares its memory path with the RISC-V host cores and the XR display engine, so a shape that issues twice the off-chip writes takes bandwidth those blocks also need, and a wearable that spends its 3\ W budget on data movement returns it as battery drain and skin-temperature throttling. Neither effect is measured here. SCALE-Sim models one accelerator against its own memory interface, so contention and thermal cost are the reason this shape earns a system-level check, not results this study can report.
:::

An architect who discovered this proxy mismatch in production (@sec-feedback-verification-trust) would not rescore these results against a new objective. The mechanism available is the one this run already used for its schema correction, a recorded preregistration amendment filed before the run it governs. Such an amendment would replace the cycles-and-utilization score with one that prices data movement, such as an energy-delay product $\text{EDP} = E_{\text{total}} \times \text{cycles}$, with $E_{\text{total}} = E_{\text{compute}} + E_{\text{SRAM}} + E_{\text{DRAM}}$ estimated by an architecture-level energy model [@WuEtAl2019Accelergy], and the amended run would be a new confirmatory study scoring power, performance, and area together rather than a rescoring of this one. No such amendment was filed here. This study reports the tie under the score it froze, and the memory axis remains a stated limitation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-proxy-mismatch
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **The proxy mismatch hides a Pareto-dominated failure.** A 1D surrogate score (such as cycles and utilization) ranks the 16 by 64 candidate exactly equal to the 32 by 32 baseline. However, plotting the candidates across two physical axes (Compute Cycles vs. Off-Chip DRAM Writes) reveals the 16 by 64 candidate is severely Pareto-dominated by the baseline when the score-ignored memory traffic is accounted for.
#| out-width: "80%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of evaluated systolic array shapes. The 32x32 baseline and 16x64 candidate are vertically aligned at about 13917 cycles on the X-axis. However, on the Y-axis (DRAM writes), the 16x64 shape is twice as high (over 400,000 writes) compared to the baseline (around 204,000 writes), showing it is dominated in actual physical cost."

import json
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

result_path = Path("../labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json")
result = json.loads(result_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

# We will just plot all evaluated runs
arm_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] in {"model", "conventional"}]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.5))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.18, right=0.95, top=0.88, bottom=0.15)

ax.set_title("Proxy Mismatch: 1D Score vs 2D Physical Reality", fontsize=7.5, pad=8)
ax.set_xlabel("Compute Cycles (lower is better)", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Off-Chip DRAM Writes (lower is better)", fontsize=6.5)

# Deduplicate points by candidate_id
seen = set()
for r in arm_runs:
    cid = r["candidate_id"]
    if cid in seen: continue
    seen.add(cid)

    cycles = r["gates"]["deadline"]["observed"]
    dram_writes = r["metrics"]["dram_writes"]

    label = cid.replace("model_baseline_", "").replace("ai_wide_", "").replace("ai_extreme_", "").replace("ai_compact_", "").replace("conventional_baseline_", "").replace("heuristic_", "")

    if "32x32" in label:
        color = COLORS["blue"]
        marker = "o"
        label_text = f"Baseline\n{label}"
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker=marker, markersize=5, color=color)
        ax.text(cycles - 500, dram_writes - 10000, label_text, color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5.5, ha="right", va="top")
    elif "16x64" in label:
        color = COLORS["red"]
        marker = "X"
        label_text = f"AI Proposal\n{label}"
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker=marker, markersize=5, color=color)
        ax.text(cycles + 300, dram_writes + 15000, label_text, color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5.5, ha="left", va="bottom")
    else:
        color = COLORS["orange"]
        marker = "s"
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker=marker, markersize=4, color=color, alpha=0.6)
        ax.text(cycles + 300, dram_writes, label, color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5, ha="left", va="center", alpha=0.7)

# Draw a dashed line showing the Pareto frontier
ax.axvline(x=13917, color=COLORS["grid"], linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, zorder=0)

ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)
for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```

[^fn-dram-traffic]: At identical cycles and utilization, the 16 by 64 shape issues 409,726 DRAM writes against the baseline's 204,863, twice as many, and about 1.6 times the DRAM accesses.

The 32 by 16 shape has higher average layer utilization than the baseline but takes far more cycles, so the composite rule ranks it worse. The 8 by 128 shape loses on both ingredients, though a reader who dislikes the composite score can still see the raw quantities and challenge the rule without rerunning the study. Whether an elongated 8 by 128 or 16 by 64 block also costs more in wire length, Network-on-Chip (NoC) routing congestion, timing closure, and global interconnect power than a compact 32 by 32 block is a reasonable hypothesis and a common one, but it is not a result of this run. SCALE-Sim performs no timing closure and no physical design, and this run enabled no energy model, so that hypothesis names the next tier of tooling this study would need, a floorplan or place-and-route estimate, rather than anything the present record can settle.

@fig-ai-study-result places the two conclusions side by side. In the left panel,
the comparison is whether either arm moves below the baseline. In the right
panel, the test is whether the mirrored shapes exchange positions after the
workload transformation.

In the left panel, the 32 by 32 baseline and 16 by 64 candidate have the same
shortest bar in both arms. No nonbaseline shape moves below the baseline. In the
right panel, 16 by 64 remains below 64 by 16 after M and N are exchanged. The
gap narrows, but the lines do not cross.

The first panel shows why no change is
warranted for the five evaluated shapes and why the two proposal arms tie on
simulator score. It does not establish that 32 by 32 is optimal across all
fifteen legal shapes or that the two methods consumed equal total effort. The
right panel probes the mechanism behind these proposals, which requires a
dedicated contrast test.

## Testing Matched Contrasts

As shown in the right panel of @fig-ai-study-result, the model predicted that 16 by 64 would beat its mirrored 64 by 16 shape on the
original workload because the wider array would align better with the supplied
N dimensions. It also predicted that exchanging M and N would reverse the
winner. This is a testable prediction because it names a direction and a
failure condition.

Each margin below compares the two shapes on one workload, so the four runs form two within-workload pairs rather than a single cross-workload comparison. On the original workload, 16 by 64 wins by 38.56 percent, with scores of
33,782.40 and 54,985.25. After transposition, it still wins by 7.57 percent,
23,530.65 to 25,458.11. The predicted reversal does not occur. The margin does narrow sharply, evidence that the transposition changed something the failed explanation cannot account for, even though the shift stopped short of a reversal.

The directional prediction therefore fails its declared contrast. Because the study's mapping semantics were unpinned (as established in @sec-executed-scale-study), this result neither shows that orientation is irrelevant nor supplies a replacement explanation. A follow-up must pin those semantics and declare a new contrast before looking for another mechanism.

## Judging Claims

With the candidate evaluations and the mechanism contrast complete, the architect can now resolve the four distinct judgments established during preregistration. The four conclusions in @tbl-study-claim-dispositions answer distinctly different questions.

| **Claim** | **Observed evidence** | **Conclusion** | **Outside this conclusion** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Architecture outcome** | Best evaluated nonbaseline ties the baseline; improvement is 0.0%. | No change under the 1 percent decision margin for the five evaluated shapes. | No claim about the ten unevaluated legal shapes, another workload, or another objective. |
| **AI contribution** | Best scores tie at four simulator calls per arm; two nonbaseline selections overlap. | Tie on the recorded simulator score. | No advantage in total effort and no broader claim about a model family. |
| **Mechanism explanation** | 16 by 64 wins on both workloads. | The directional prediction fails its declared contrast. | No causally isolated replacement explanation, especially without pinned mapping semantics. |
| **Stopping decision** | No selected candidate clears the decision margin, and post-result replacement is prohibited. | Stop the bounded search and keep 32 by 32 as the status quo for the evaluated set. | No claim that 32 by 32 is optimal among all fifteen legal shapes. |

: **The four judgments have different conclusions.** The architecture outcome, AI contribution, mechanism explanation, and stopping decision remain separate. {#tbl-study-claim-dispositions tbl-colwidths="[19,31,18,32]"}

The first row asks whether any new shape warrants a change under the local
score. The second asks whether the model found an advantage over the heuristic
under the same simulator-call budget. The third tests only the model's
explanation. The fourth records what the architect does next. Each conclusion
follows from different evidence.

A different run could split them. A candidate that cleared the margin would set the architecture outcome to a change and still leave the stopping decision at stop, if the evaluation budget were spent or the gain did not justify the cost of verifying it. In this run no candidate cleared the margin, so the outcome and the stopping decision point the same way, and the mechanism verdict stands apart from both.

The frozen protocol permits no post-result replacement, and no candidate clears the decision margin, so this bounded search stops here. The evidence warrants retaining 32 by 32 as the status quo for the five evaluated shapes because a nonbaseline tie does not justify change when the preregistration names no compensating benefit. Further evaluation is warranted only if a broader architecture decision needs more evidence, perhaps from a broader workload, another dataflow, pinned mapping semantics, a calibrated memory model, or implementation-adjacent constraints. The present evidence does not authorize RTL, tapeout, or a system intent decision.

## Packaging the Study {#sec-ai-study-archive}

The retained replay package contains the frozen context, complete model
response, public-safe provenance, exact simulator inputs, raw summary reports,
parsed results, hashes, tests, and replay code. This study carries no proprietary PDK data or RTL, so making the package public-safe required only removing local pathnames. In a production setting, the same step would also strip confidential inputs before release, so a reviewer can check provenance without exposing protected material. The package is pinned to a single recorded commit rather than a mutable branch.

### Mapping Artifacts to Review Questions

Each retained artifact answers a specific review question
(@tbl-study-archive).

| **Artifact** | **What it lets a reviewer check** |
| --- | --- |
| **Preregistration** | Whether claims, candidates per arm, rejection criteria, score, decision margin, repair limit, contrast, and decision boundary predate inference and simulation. |
| **Model prompt, schema, and full response** | What context the model saw, which authority it lacked, and whether the printed proposals and prediction match the retained response. |
| **Provenance record** | Requested model alias, interface, timestamps, exposed settings, usage, response hash, pre-inference error, and unavailable identity fields. |
| **Fixed aspect-ratio heuristic** | Whether its ordering was deterministic and fixed before model or simulator output. |
| **Reference evaluations and execution provenance** | Exact topology, layout, SCALE-Sim configuration, raw run locations, parsed metrics, rejection results, and conclusions for all twelve evaluations. |
| **Reference manifest and replay** | Whether retained files match their hashes and a network-free rerun regenerates every stable input, report, metric, and result. |

: **Every review question maps to a retained artifact:** these files do not establish that the simulator is accurate or the workload representative, but they preserve the declared run so reviewers can examine those assumptions. {#tbl-study-archive tbl-colwidths="[26,64]"}

### Three Levels of Verification

These artifacts support verification across three distinct levels of scrutiny, as categorized in @tbl-verification-levels.

| **Verification Level** | **Action** | **What It Establishes** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Replay** | Rerunning the exact same simulator logs with the same deterministic inputs. | Establishes that the recorded execution is unaltered and the math adds up. |
| **Reproduction** | Rerunning the AI agent with the same prompt and seed. | Highlights model drift, API changes, and non-determinism. |
| **Independent validation** | A different team building a different model or testbench to evaluate the same architectural claim in RTL. | Establishes that the architectural mechanism survives an independent implementation and a different set of modeling assumptions, removing shared-toolchain artifacts as an explanation. It remains a pre-silicon result, since physical behavior is established only by measurement on fabricated hardware. |

: **Replay proves reproducibility, not fidelity or correctness:** true architectural trust requires independent validation, while replay guarantees only that the study faithfully executed its own declared loop. {#tbl-verification-levels tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

### Verifying the Replay

The preregistration and model artifacts show what was fixed before inference.
The raw reports and parsed results show what SCALE-Sim returned. The manifest
and replay code connect the reported numbers back to the retained files. The
pinned commit identifies one immutable repository state instead of a mutable
branch name. Together, those records let another architect check the declared
computation without implying that SCALE-Sim is accurate enough for a different
claim or that the workload represents the full system intent.

Offline replay needs no network account or model credential. It verifies the
reference, reruns all twelve evaluations, and compares their stable inputs,
summary reports, metrics, and hashes. Large deterministic access traces are
regenerated rather than archived. That substitution rests on an assumption worth
stating, that regeneration under the pinned simulator version and configuration
yields byte-identical traces to those the reported metrics were computed from.
The assumption is checkable and was not separately checked here, so a replay that
disagrees on a metric should suspect the trace before it suspects the metric.

An optional provider-neutral live adapter writes to a separate output directory
and checks the requested model alias. That check does not recover the exact
provider revision or digest used for the recorded call. The adapter halts if the
runtime or credential is unavailable, the response is invalid, or a proposed
geometry is illegal. It never changes the recorded reference results. Commands
and failure details remain in the companion rather than the printed chapter.

Replay confirms the recorded computation under the retained code, inputs, and
environment. It is not an independent reproduction because it shares the same
runner, simulator, workload, score, and assumptions. It does not validate
SCALE-Sim against measurements from fabricated silicon, establish workload
representativeness, justify the local score or thresholds, resolve the missing
mapping semantics, or predict the output of another model call. Those are new
claims requiring new evidence.

## Open Research Questions

Four loose ends survive the bounded study's clean null result. Each marks a place where the worked mechanics stopped short of a general claim.

**Theme 1: The Memory-Blind Proxy.** The local score combined only cycles and utilization, so it rated two shapes identical while their off-chip write traffic differed twofold. Pricing that gap afterward took published per-access energy constants and an order-of-magnitude caveat, which is a long way from a term a selection rule could carry while the search is still running.

- How can a selection score admit an energy-relevant axis such as off-chip write traffic without an unvalidated energy term overwhelming the well-understood ingredients it joins?
- What would establish that an architecture-level energy model is faithful enough to score candidates inside the loop rather than price a decision after it is made?

**Theme 2: The Unpinned Mechanism.** The record fixed the dataflow but never bound the workload's loop dimensions to the array's spatial dimensions, so the contrast tested the completeness of the prompt rather than the model's architectural reasoning.

- How can a study pin the mapping between a workload's loop dimensions and an accelerator's spatial dimensions so that a directional-mechanism prediction becomes a causally isolated test rather than an ungrounded one?
- How can a generator's stated mechanism be tested separately from the correctness of its proposal, so that a sound candidate arriving with a false explanation is recorded as exactly that?

**Theme 3: Resolving Power Before the Run.** Two competent proposers converging on the same candidates in a small legal space produced a tie that was likely before either arm ran. The evaluation was deterministic and noise-free, so no sampling noise entered the scores. The proposer was not, since repeated model calls define a distribution over proposals, and what a fixed contrast could not overcome was the small legal space rather than the absence of a sampling distribution.

- How can a study establish before execution whether its comparison can distinguish two proposers at all, when the candidate space is small, discrete, and free of sampling noise?
- Which candidates in a bounded search are settleable in closed form before any expensive evaluation is spent, and how would a loop identify them automatically?

**Theme 4: The Sample of One.** One recorded model call, replayed under its own tooling, cannot speak for a model family or count as an independent reproduction, and the checks that would have rejected an illegal or over-cycle candidate never fired at all.

- What sampling budget across model calls would let a study report a population-level result about a model family rather than the single-call comparison this one supports?
- What second and independent implementation would separate a genuine architecture finding from an artifact of the shared runner, simulator, workload, and score?
- What adversarial candidate set would exercise a study's declared rejection checks in the rejecting direction, so that a check which has never fired is demonstrated rather than assumed?

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="The Traceability Mandate"}
A generated candidate is only as valuable as the reproducible tool path and evidence record that accompanies it. The architecture environment must capture the exact intent, baseline, constraints, and tool telemetry for every run, ensuring that negative evidence and failed candidates are preserved to map the boundaries of the design space.
:::

The open questions of proxy mismatches, unpinned physical mappings, and single-shot evaluation limits highlight where this localized SLAM study stops short of full system verification. These are not just academic curiosities; they are the exact physical and statistical barriers that prevent AI from scaling across the stack. In the next chapter (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack), we will elevate these localized boundaries and examine how these design loops compound when scaled across the entire architecture, from software mapping down to standard-cell physical design.


This bounded integration study ends with a tie against the baseline, where the model and fixed aspect-ratio heuristic selected five unique datapath shapes from fifteen legal shapes. Because no evaluated nonbaseline shape cleared the 1 percent decision margin over 32 by 32, the record retains the 32 by 32 baseline. This no-change outcome carries weight because the decision rule was fixed before execution, not because any candidate was exposed as flawed; the nonbaseline shapes tied or ranked worse, and none was ruled out as defective.

The study also demonstrates how to evaluate AI fairly. The declared contrast tested the model's directional prediction, which failed to produce the anticipated reversal. Because the simulator environment, scoring rules, prompt structure, and decision margins were locked before execution, any post-hoc rationalization or baseline shopping would be visible against the recorded rule rather than silent.

Catching schema errors before simulation shows why structured output must be validated into legal simulator actions. One small experiment does not validate the complete Architecture 2.0 discipline, but it shows that an adopted proposal can be tied to measured performance rather than to a persuasive model output.

::: {.callout-carry-forward}
- **Carry forward:** Freeze the workload, score, decision margin, and budget before the first candidate is measured. Keep the architecture outcome, AI contribution, mechanism explanation, and stopping decision separate. Validate structured AI intent into legal simulator actions. Test a directional explanation against a matched contrast declared before any result is seen, and treat the explanation as unsupported when the contrast does not move in the predicted direction, even when the compared conditions separate cleanly. Preserve every evaluated candidate, even when the final result is a no-change tie or an unsupported mechanism explanation.
- **Reader test:** Can another architect distinguish replay of the fixed computation from independent reproduction, identify the missing mapping semantics, and explain why stopping does not imply optimality?
- **Up next:** The same loop must now work across very different decisions, and what changes is not the size of the artifact. @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack classifies the next decision by how slow it is to evaluate, how many interfaces it spans, how hard it is to reverse, and what it costs to get wrong, then sets what the AI may do and who may let the result advance from that classification rather than from the artifact's name.
:::
